column2: Ping sends an ICMP Echo request and waits for a reply. Success confirms round-trip IP connectivity at that moment. ICMP also reports forwarding problems, such as destination unreachable or hop limit exceeded. This limit is called TTL in IPv4 and Hop Limit in IPv6. A ping reply does not guarantee that HTTP is allowed.
A firewall can allow ping and block TCP/80. In that case, the host replies, but the page never arrives.
Compare the source, destination, TTL or Hop Limit, and result of a ping.
Use a low hop limit on a routed network and examine which device returns the error.
RTT is calculated from the virtual clock, latencies, and event processing.
Routes and gateways

The router looks for the route with the most specific prefix that matches the destination. That route defines the outgoing interface and, when necessary, the next hop. The default route covers destinations without a more specific match. The reply also needs a return path.
A /24 route takes precedence over a /0 default route for the same destination. A route that exists only in the outbound direction can leave the connection without a reply.
Check the routing table and identify the outgoing interface for each packet.
Remove a return route and compare the events before and after.
Connected, static, and learned routes are used in the engine's actual forwarding.

VLANs separate broadcast domains on the same switch. An access port associates frames with the configured VLAN. A trunk carries multiple VLANs, usually identified by 802.1Q tags. Routing is required for different VLANs to communicate.
Two PCs in VLAN 20 can end up isolated if the trunk between the switches does not allow that VLAN.
Compare the hosts' access VLAN with the VLANs allowed on the trunk.
Open a frame on the link between switches and observe the 802.1Q tag.
The VLAN takes part in MAC learning and forwarding decisions; it is not just a visual label.

An SVI is an IP interface associated with a VLAN on the switch. A subinterface divides a physical port into logical interfaces, each with its own VLAN. Either can serve as a gateway; the device must have routing enabled, and the VLANs must reach the interface.
The VLAN 20 SVI can be the 192.168.20.1 gateway, while the VLAN 30 SVI serves another subnet.
Compare the host's gateway with the address of the SVI or subinterface.
Check ip routing and whether the VLANs are carried over the links.
Logical interfaces use the ports and forwarding of the simulated topology.
STP/RSTP and loop prevention

Redundant links between switches can cause a frame to circulate indefinitely. STP elects a root and blocks paths that would form loops. RSTP speeds up the transition to another path when a failure occurs. A connected link can be blocked for data traffic as a result of that decision.
In a triangle of switches, one of the paths does not forward data until it is needed for recovery.
Compare the root, the cost, and the forwarding/discarding state of the ports.
Shut down an uplink and watch the path change before repeating the ping.
Port states and BPDUs are part of the simulation; reconvergence depends on the processed events.
PVST and MSTP: per-VLAN or per-instance trees

PVST maintains one spanning tree per VLAN, allowing different roots and paths to be chosen. MSTP groups VLANs into instances that share a tree. Switches in the same MST region must agree on the name, revision, and VLAN mapping; different configurations create region boundaries.
VLANs 10 and 20 can use different uplinks with distinct roots in PVST, or share the same path if they belong to the same MST instance.
Compare roots and port states per VLAN or instance.
Change a switch's VLAN mapping and check the resulting region and paths.
The engine models instances, states, and BPDUs; changing the mode alters the topology's spanning trees.
LACP and link aggregation

LACP negotiates which ports can join an aggregated logical link. At least one side must start the negotiation in active mode; two passive sides never start it. The members must be compatible. If one member is lost, the remaining members can keep the bundle operational.
Two cables between switches are not automatically combined into a single link; the negotiation and configuration must match.
Check the selected members and the active/passive modes.
Disable a member and start a new connection to test the remaining path.
Aggregation is modeled as negotiation and forwarding; it does not reproduce every behavior of an ASIC.
VRRP and gateway redundancy

VRRP presents a virtual IP as the hosts' gateway. The routers elect one of them to be responsible for that IP; another can take over if it fails. Priority influences the election. Tracking lowers the priority when a monitored interface or route loses connectivity.
The PC keeps the same gateway while responsibility for it moves between two routers.
Compare the virtual IP, priority, and state of each router.
Cause an uplink failure and test a new connection after the election.
The implementation covers IPv4 VRRP and tracking on the virtual clock.
VRF: separate routing tables

A VRF maintains an independent routing table. The incoming interface determines which table is used to look up the packet. This allows networks with overlapping IP addresses to coexist without mixing traffic. Having a route in one VRF does not make it available in another.
BLUE and RED can use the same server IP and reply over different paths.
Check the routes and interfaces of each VRF.
Send traffic through both tables and compare which server replies.
Routes are not exchanged automatically between VRFs; each flow uses its own table.
DHCPv4 and leases

DHCP provides the client with an address, mask, and other options through a temporary lease. The initial exchange uses Discover, Offer, Request, and ACK. A relay forwards the messages when the server is on another network; the server uses that information to choose the appropriate pool.
Two clients can receive different addresses from the same pool and use the gateway provided by the server.
Set the interface to DHCP and follow the four messages.
Compare the pool, lease, gateway, and renewal on the client and the server.
Pools, reservations, relay, expiration, and conflicts are evaluated through the lab's events.
DNS: names and records

DNS looks up records associated with a name. An A record maps to an IPv4 address, AAAA to an IPv6 address, and a CNAME points to another name. The cache avoids repeating queries while the TTL is valid. Resolving a name does not confirm that the service at that address is available.
app.lab can resolve to 192.168.10.20 and still not respond to HTTP if TCP/80 is blocked.
Query a name and examine the question, answer, and records.
Repeat the query and check the cache and TTL before changing the record.
The server and caches are local to the simulation; queries are not sent to the Internet.

TCP establishes a connection with SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK. Data is sequenced and acknowledged; losses can cause retransmission. The window and congestion control limit sending. HTTP uses this connection to request a resource and receive a response: the handshake alone does not prove that the application responded.
A GET request travels over TCP/80; you can follow the connection setup and the HTTP response separately.
Open a connection and compare SYN, ACK, data, and FIN in the packets.
Introduce loss and observe in-flight segments, retransmissions, and the HTTP result.
TCP has persisted timers and states; HTTP is an application subset implemented for the lab.
UDP and ports

UDP delivers datagrams identified by source and destination ports, without establishing a connection or acknowledging delivery. The application must handle loss and retries when necessary. DNS, DHCP, and several monitoring services use UDP, each with its own rules.
A DNS query can go unanswered if the return datagram is lost, even with the link up.
Open a packet and compare the source and destination ports.
Introduce loss and check the timeout or retry performed by the application.
Datagrams traverse links, routes, ACLs, and NAT the same way as other IP packets.
OSPF and path cost

OSPF forms adjacencies and exchanges information about the links in the area. Each router calculates paths based on cumulative cost and installs the resulting routes. Finding a neighbor is not enough: the adjacency, the advertisements, and the forwarding table must all be correct.
After a failure, a route can move to a higher-cost path that still reaches the destination.
Compare neighbors, adjacency, and learned routes.
Disable a link and check the new route before testing HTTP.
Areas and advertisements are modeled with simulator PDUs; there is no session with external routers.
RIP and hop count

RIP advertises networks and their hop count to neighbors. The router selects the usable advertisements, adds the local hop, and installs the routes. Timers remove stale information; unreachable-route advertisements help propagate a failure. The usable limit is 15 hops.
If a neighbor stops advertising a network, the route can remain for a while until it expires.
Compare the received advertisements with the hop count of the installed route.
Stop the protocol and advance virtual time to observe the expiration.
The engine models RIPv2, filters, and timers; it does not query external networks.
BGP and advertisement policies

BGP exchanges prefixes between neighbors and applies policies to select and advertise paths. AS_PATH records the autonomous systems traversed and helps prevent loops. An established session does not guarantee traffic: the prefix must be accepted and the next hop must be reachable.
A filter can remove a network from the advertisements while the TCP session between the routers stays up.
Check the session, the received prefixes, and AS_PATH.
Change a policy and compare the installed route with the result of a new connection.
BGP uses typed messages over the simulated network and does not interoperate with external sessions.

IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses. NDP resolves neighbors and checks for duplicates with DAD. Routers send RAs to advertise prefixes and gateways; with SLAAC, the host forms an address from the prefix. An address that is still tentative is not ready for normal use.
A PC can learn the prefix from an RA and resolve the gateway's MAC address through NDP before sending the ping.
Compare tentative/preferred addresses, RAs, and the neighbor table.
Send an IPv6 ping between subnets and observe the Hop Limit.
NDP replaces ARP in this flow; TCP and UDP over IPv6 use the same forwarding decisions.
DHCPv6 and prefix delegation

DHCPv6 can provide addresses and options, or delegate a prefix to another network. It does not provide the default gateway: that role belongs to RAs. IA_NA represents an address association; IA_PD represents a delegated-prefix association.
A client can have an address leased by DHCPv6 and still need an RA to reach another subnet.
Compare the address/prefix leases on the client and the server.
Check the RA and the default route separately from the DHCPv6 lease.
Leases, renewal, and relay use IPv6 datagrams in the topology.
Wi-Fi: association, signal, and authentication

The client must find a compatible AP and complete authentication before exchanging data over the wireless network. The SSID, security settings, and credentials must match. Distance, channel, and interference affect signal, loss, and capacity; associating is no substitute for configuring IP.
A laptop can see the SSID and still fail to associate because of an incorrect key. After associating, it still needs to reach its gateway.
Check the association, key, channel, and signal strength.
Move the client farther away or change the channel, and compare traffic loss.
The radio is a coverage/interference model; it does not control a real Wi-Fi adapter.

A wireless LAN controller (WLC) centralizes AP configuration. CAPWAP carries control traffic and, in centralized mode, client data to the controller. The AP must reach the WLC over the IP network before it receives a usable WLAN.
An AP can have its radio on and still not offer the expected WLAN because it cannot reach the controller.
Check discovery, the AP session, and the WLAN profiles on the WLC.
Break the IP path to the controller and observe the effect on client traffic.
Control and data traffic travel through the modeled network; there is no external CAPWAP interoperability.
Wireless mesh network

In a mesh, APs form wireless neighbor relationships to forward data to a root or exit point. The link between APs is separate from client association. The mesh identity, security, and path must be correct to avoid a client that is associated but cannot access the destination network.
A client can associate with a remote AP whose mesh path to the root is unavailable.
Compare the neighbors and the path to the mesh root.
Power off an intermediate AP and check whether another usable path exists.
Mesh discovery and forwarding are limited to the engine's rules.
VPN and transport network

A VPN tunnel carries inner packets across an outer network called the underlay. The peers must reach each other and negotiate compatible parameters before protecting data. A route through the tunnel interface does not fix a failure in the route to the other peer.
An incorrect key can prevent negotiation even when the outer addresses have IP connectivity.
Compare the peers, credentials, and negotiation state.
Open the outer traffic and compare it with the destination of the encapsulated packet.
Encryption and states are modeled in the lab; the tunnel does not connect to a real VPN.
SD-WAN and path selection

SD-WAN distributes policies and chooses transports based on the application and measured conditions. RTT, loss, and availability can change which tunnel is used. A received policy does not create connectivity: the transports and routes of each tunnel must also work.
HTTP can switch transports when the first path no longer meets the policy's loss threshold.
Compare the received policy and the transport measurements.
Cause a failure and observe the path of a new connection.
Measurements and policies depend on virtual events and the configured tunnels.
QoS, classification, and queuing

When an outgoing interface receives more traffic than it can transmit, frames wait in queues or are dropped. QoS classifies that traffic and defines how the queues share capacity. DSCP is a classification marking; marking a packet does not increase link capacity.
A priority class can wait less while another accumulates drops on a congested outgoing interface.
Reduce the capacity and compare marking, queues, and drops.
Change the policy and observe the delay and the number of frames transmitted.
Queues and their capacity are simplified; they do not represent specific hardware.
MPLS and labels

MPLS maps traffic to a label-switched path. The ingress router pushes a label, intermediate devices look up the LFIB and swap it, and the egress router removes the encapsulation. The mapping of incoming label, outgoing label, and next interface must form a complete path.
A wrong label on the intermediate router can break the path even when the IP routes at the edges are correct.
Follow the push, swap, and pop operations on the packets.
Compare the observed labels with the LFIB entries.
MPLS paths are configured statically; the model has no LDP/RSVP.

VXLAN encapsulates an Ethernet frame in UDP to cross an IP network. The VNI identifies the logical network, and the VTEPs perform encapsulation and delivery. The local VLANs can differ, but the VNI, peers, and underlay connectivity must match.
Two switches can extend a local network over UDP/4789 without using the same VLAN number at each end.
Compare the VNI and the VTEP addresses.
Open the outer UDP packet and the Ethernet frame carried inside it.
VXLAN uses the model's actual links and IP routes, without creating external connectivity.
EVPN and MAC/IP location

EVPN uses BGP advertisements to indicate where a MAC/IP can be reached. Route targets determine which advertisements a network imports. This makes it possible to direct traffic to the correct VTEP; an active BGP session with mismatched route targets can leave destinations without a route.
The remote MAC is advertised by one switch, but the other does not import it because it uses a different route target.
Compare MAC/IP advertisements and their route targets.
Fix the import and observe the VTEP chosen for the traffic.
The model covers a MAC/IP subset, not every EVPN service or redundancy mode.
802.1X, RADIUS, and network access

802.1X controls a client's access to the network. The client is the supplicant, the switch/AP acts as the authenticator, and the RADIUS server evaluates authentication. Authorization can open the port and assign a VLAN. In enterprise Wi-Fi, PEAP/TLS also requires validating certificates and credentials.
A connected cable does not guarantee that data gets through: the port can remain unauthorized until the server accepts the client.
Compare the port state before and after the RADIUS response.
Test incorrect credentials and check the resulting VLAN and authorization.
Network credentials belong to the lab; they are not the account used to sign in to shLab.
AAA and TACACS+: terminal access

AAA combines authentication, authorization, and accounting. TACACS+ can verify who accesses a device and which commands that person can run. Being authenticated does not mean being authorized to change configurations; the policy must also permit the action.
A user can view routes and be denied when trying to change an interface.
Compare privilege levels and command policies on the server.
Run a read-only command and a configuration command, then check the accounting records.
Authorization controls the terminal of the simulated devices and does not change the application account.
